newsitem.title: switzerland: Swiss apologise to Jews, review fast compensation.
newsitem.headline: Swiss apologise to Jews, review fast compensation.

text.p: The Swiss economics minister apologised on Wednesday for labelling as "blackmail" compensation demands for Holocaust victims, backing his country away from confrontation with world Jewish groups.
The Federal Council, or cabinet, also pledged to examine whether it could soon pay Jews to make amends for Switzerland's anti-Jewish refugee policy in World War Two and purchases of looted Nazi gold.

Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delmuraz apologised in a letter to World Jewish Congress (WJC) President Edgar Bronfman, saying he was "very sorry that I offended your feelings as well as those of...the Jewish community at large.

"I assure you this was not my intention. The information on which I had based my statement regarding the fund was inaccurate," he added, referring to a Holocaust memorial fund under discussion between Berne and Jewish groups.

The WJC and its allies want compensation for what they call Swiss wrongdoing, chiefly charges that Swiss banks hoarded wealth left by Jews killed by the Nazis. Berne's turning back of most Jewish refugees as the Holocaust raged also irks them.

Jewish leaders welcomed the apology as a return to the dialogue they broke off when Delamuraz made his remarks in a newspaper interview on December 31 -- his last day in the one-year rotating Swiss presidency.
The WJC and Israel's quasi-governmental Jewish Agency had threatened a boycott of Swiss banks if Berne did not apologise.
The Swiss government said Bronfman responded by fax within hours, acknowledging receipt of Delamuraz's apology and adding:
"I look forward to return to constructive work together with the Swiss authorities and the Swiss banks, to resolve outstanding questions which will further our goals of truth and justice."
Swiss Jewish Federation leader Rolf Bloch said Delamuraz could have phrased his apology more strongly but added: "If this reestablishes the dialogue, then that is a good thing."

Delamuraz angered world Jewish groups and Israeli politicians by saying Jewish organisations were demanding 250 million Swiss francs ($180 million) from Berne and calling the idea "extortion and blackmail".
WJC leaders denied having proposed any sums to the Swiss. Thomas Borer, Swiss special ambassador for the Jewish assets issue, has in turn denied floating the figure.

The cabinet asked a panel of historians it charged last month with a probe of the Swiss wartime role to give first priority to Nazi gold purchases and a refugee policy that turned back thousands of Jews to face near-certain death.
The statement appeared to back up forecasts by Berne officials that the government planned a fast financial gesture.

At the same time, Swiss banks faced a new controversy after Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) said an employee had destroyed old records in possible violation of a federal decree protecting evidence that could lead to lost Jewish wealth.
"This event is very sensitive politically," prosecutor Peter Cosnadey said about the case, which he is investigating.
UBS called the incident "a regrettable accident" but other bankers said the revelation would reinforce widespread suspicion of Swiss banks among Jewish and foreign critics.

"It is more than merely regrettable that the damage will affect other (banks) and not least the image of Switzerland, which has already been shaken badly enough," the conservative newspaper Neue Zuericher Zeitung commented.
